utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case IT-97-25-T, the Prosecutor versus Milorad Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not going to apologise for being late because that clock is fast, but I suppose it's the one by which we should operate. Yes, Ms. Kuo -- I'm sorry, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us that you saw the two villages of Paunci -- the two villages of Paunci and Filipovici burning, and can you tell us when? Do you recall when that happened, the date?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: That happened towards the end of April 1992. It could have been the 25th or the 26th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And besides the houses being burned, did you see persons being killed?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I saw the soldiers taking the military buildings and facilities in Filipovici, and when they lined up a group of people within the military compound there I saw that they singled out a few of them, four or five, I think. After that I heard shots. I saw some buses that were there, seems to me that there were two. There was a military transporter as well. And then these buses set out towards Foca. In the village of Gornji Paunovci before that, I saw soldiers who were forcing a woman towards the Drina River, and after that a soldier shot that woman from a rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And yesterday you also mentioned that the village of Josanica -- actually, the two villages of Josanica were attacked as well. When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: That happened a day later. I was watching as the buses full of soldiers were coming into Josanica. I counted about 12 trucks then, I believe. These were military trucks that had benches on the side where there could -- they could seat about 15 soldiers, so it could have been about 300 soldiers altogether. They started shooting all over the village, and I saw the first houses that belonged to Muslims, Bosniaks, being torched. These are houses at the entrance into Josanica. I know exactly which families they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the other houses where Muslims were living, were they destroyed or torched as well on that day?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I think that the vast majority of the houses in the village of Josanica were burned down. Perhaps one or two have remained unburned. After that, they attacked the village of Ribari - that's the place where my house is - and all the houses in that village were torched. I saw my own house burning, and I saw soldiers in uniform approaching my house, entering it, torching it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were Serb houses burnt down or damaged in any way?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you wounded at one point in time?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I was wounded on a hillock above the village of Karadzici on the 19th of April, when the shelling started. I was wounded by a shrapnel coming from a shell that had fallen near me. I was wounded in both legs, in the knee area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you doing when you were wounded? You said you were on a hill. What were you doing there?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I was trying to find my brother and my brother-in-law, that is to say, my wife's brother. When the shelling started, I was in a weekend cottage where there were refugees, my wife, children, my mother, and other women and children and old people from the village. When the shelling started, I had set out for that hillock, looking for the two of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After being wounded, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I tried to go down towards that village, that is to say, the weekend cottage where my wife and children were. However, I didn't manage to do so. Halil Merkez was with me, an elderly man. He was wounded, but his wounds were less serious. He tried to drag me down to that weekend cottage on a tree branch. However, he didn't manage to. So then I crawled to a stream by myself, and I hid in the bushes there or, rather, in a pile of leaves. There were oak trees there, and then I found oak leaves and covered myself with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you arrested at a point in time on that day?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Not on that day. Two of my sisters-in-law came to get me, and they brought me down to that weekend cottage. We spent the night at the weekend cottage. In the morning, the Chetniks came to the door and arrested me. So that was the 30th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said the Chetniks arrested you. Did you know them? Could you say who arrested you, neighbours or soldiers from other areas?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: All the soldiers that entered the weekend cottage were my neighbours, most of them. I knew them. Only one of them was not from Bosnia. Judging by his accent, by the way he spoke, I came to the conclusion that he was from Serbia. I knew all the rest from before, and I had even treated some of them, as a doctor, while they were in hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you the only person arrested on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: No. Halil Merkez was also arrested with me. Later on, I found out that my wife's brother had been arrested too, my brother-in-law, as well as a friend of his.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name of your wife's brother?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Nedzad Delic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other gentleman that was arrested somewhat later, what was his name?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Adnan Dzaferspahic is the name of the other young man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These people, these soldiers that arrested you, did they tell you why you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: At first, they were very harsh. The soldier from Serbia cocked his rifle. It was a PAP rifle. He put a bullet into his rifle. I lay immobile on a couch. He pointed the rifle at my stomach, putting the tip of the rifle actually against my stomach, and asked me whether I had any weapons, and he said if he found any weapons in the house, he would kill everyone. He saw my doctor's bag that was there, and then he said things like -- that I had come to treat balijas there, that he'd kill me, whatever. I think that Marko Matovic, a soldier I knew well, commanded this attack. I came to the conclusion that he commanded this attack because he looked somewhat different. He had a beret, an olive-green/grey uniform and also a Serbian flag on the left-hand side of his cap. They did not tell me why they were arresting me, what the reason for my arrest was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I was taken to hospital, to the Foca hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Merkez, was he also taken there?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: He was too, except we were taken in different cars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I stayed until the 21st of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this time period, were you treated normally as a patient?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I lay at the same ward where I had worked before that, surgery, that is. The anaesthesiologist was a Bosniak lady, Adina Spahic. She told me one morning that I had to have surgery performed on me. I was immobile, and I had to have a nerve operated, and I agreed. I said that I trusted them and that I agreed. So I was operated on two days after I was brought to hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you stayed there until the 21st of May, 1992. Where were you taken afterwards? On that day, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: After that, they took me to the KP Dom in Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you recovered already from your wounds by that time?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: No, no. I could not walk. I couldn't stand on my feet; I had to use crutches. Some additional examinations had to be carried out; however, this was not possible at the Foca hospital then. I was transferred -- or rather, I was supposed to be transferred to the rehabilitation recuperation ward, but the head of this ward did not agree to admit me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Merkez stay as long in the hospital, or was he taken away earlier than you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: He was taken to the hospital -- no, I'm sorry, the KP Dom earlier. When I arrived there, I already found him in the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took you to the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Two soldiers of the so-called special police, as they had introduced themselves. They were wearing military uniforms. One of them was Slavisa Jovic, I know him; and the other one is Maidov, his nickname is Zeco. I also knew him from before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said a special police. Do you mean military police or any other body?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: They introduced themselves. They said, "We're the special military police, and we've come to take you to the KP Dom." They said that they had orders to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they indicate who gave them the orders to do that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I asked them directly, "Who gave you these orders?" They said that they could not tell, that they had to do it, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I stayed for a total of 479 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what date, on what date did you leave? Do you recall the date?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I left the KP Dom on the 12th of August, 1993, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the KP Dom, who received you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Slavko Koroman was at the gate then. I had known him from before. He allowed me to bring in the things I had had with me. We even talked. He asked me whether I had weapons, whether I had a pistol; however, he did not beat me. He was correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you why you were taken to the KP Dom and how long you would stay?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: He didn't say anything. I didn't ask him anything, either. I didn't ask him how long I'd stay or anything like that. At any rate, he didn't tell me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he wearing when he [sic] arrived, what kind of clothes?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I think he wore the kind of uniform that was worn by the former policemen in the KP Dom. That was a blue uniform, a light blue uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the KP Dom, were soldiers around? Did you see any soldiers in front of the KP Dom or in the compound?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Then I did not see any soldiers within the compound of the KP Dom. At the reception office I saw some men who were probably guards. They wore olive-green/gray uniforms and also light blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you registered when you arrived at the KP Dom? I mean, were your particulars taken down?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: My name is not on a single list. I was never registered by any organisation or any service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken within the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I was taken to Room 16.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in which part of the building is it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: That room is within the prison compound, in the central part. It is on the ground floor. The windows of this room face the administration building. After the few steps at the entrance, one enters this room on the left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. How long did you stay in Room 16? Approximately, we do not need the exact date.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps about six months, but I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall to which other rooms you were taken while you were detained?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I was in Room 18, which is just above Room 16. I was on the second floor in the right-hand block in a room there, I don't know the number of that room; and on the second floor in the left-hand block, but again, I can't remember the number of that room either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the second floor, how do you count? Do you count the ground floor as separate, or is the ground floor the first floor? Maybe I -- maybe we'll use a photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, do you use the European or American style? I think that's probably the real issue. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is the ground floor the first floor, or is the next floor up the first floor?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether in Europe the ground floor is the first floor or not, but, I mean, where I come from the ground floor is the ground floor. So I was on the first floor, speaking in European terms, on the first floor in the left-hand block and on the first floor in the right-hand block. In American terms, this would be the second floor, then, I imagine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. When you arrived in Room 16, were there already detainees there? You already mentioned Mr. Merkez. Was he in Room 16 together with other detainees already?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was in Room 16. I found about 30 detainees there. I knew many of them personally. I didn't know others, though. Some I had seen for the first time, but all of them were Muslims, Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were others brought to your room, Room 16, after your arrival?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that most of the detainees in Room 16 were -- the largest number was 77, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that they were all Muslims. The age of these detainees, from which age to which did it vary?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: The range was very big. I think the youngest one was about 15 or 16. Fifteen, 15, actually, a young boy from Miljevina. And the oldest one in my room, in Room 16, was Hamdija Hadzimuratovic, I think. He was almost 70, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were doctors or other medical staff among the detainees in Room 16? And if you look at the list before you, tell us names. Please look at the list and use code numbers if you find someone from the list.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: As for medical staff in Room 16, there was detainee FWS-76, then detainee Aziz Torlak, who had been transferred from the neighbouring room to my room. He was a doctor. Also, there was a nurse, a male nurse. We called him Zibac. He had worked in the hospital with me. I can't remember whether there were any other male nurses with me at that point in time in Room 16, but I'm sure about these two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And later on? Do you recall any other medical person that you were detained with later on?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Later, when I was transferred to another room, I saw detainee FWS-111, and for a while we were in the same room. I also met a dentist, Dr. Said, who had worked in the KP Dom before the war. I met Emir Mandzo, whom they had brought to Room 16 from work. And they told me that Dr. Asima Pilav was in the KP Dom with her family before that and that Dr. Spahic Kasim had spent a night there as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And were sick people among you? Do you recall any sick people? I'm not talking about people being beaten in the KP Dom or receiving injuries in the KP Dom. I'm speaking about sick people, other sick people.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: There were a lot of old, sick people, even in Room 16 where I was. I remember Muradif Konjo, for example, an elderly man. He was over 60 years old. He had high blood pressure. I remember detainee FWS-104, also an elderly person. He was sick. I remember Abid Sahovic, a detainee who was a retired person as well. He had problems with his liver, bleedings, things like that. In other rooms there were other detainees who were old and in pretty bad shape and who needed medical care. For example, detainee FWS-172, who had worked in the hospital and who was quite sick. He was just about to retire, actually. Then detainee FWS-182, who had problems with his stomach, with an ulcer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any detainee who had an injury or disease in his face so that he could not eat? Do you recall any person?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that detainee. He was in my room. His name is Ramiz Dzano. They called him Kengo. His face had been injured. He was a neighbour of mine. I had known him from before. His face was wounded by a shell. And that's what he told me too. He told me he was wounded by a shell. He also said to me that he had been wounded in the town of Foca, that he was taken to hospital and that from the hospital he was brought to the KP Dom. He could not eat. His lips were cut up. He had injuries in his mouth, so he could only drink water through a straw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any detainees in your room or in other rooms that had been involved in a traffic accident before the war? Do you recall anyone?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. I think it's the Dzozo brothers from Gorazde. They were in my room. There were two other men together with them in my room. I can't remember now, but I know that those two brothers are called Dzozo. They had been injured in a car accident. They skidded off the road into a ditch and then we were transferred to a hospital and then from the hospital they were transferred to the KP Dom. These were light injuries, except for the fact that one of the Djozo brothers had problems with his jaw and he could not chew his food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These detainees that you just mentioned and that were sick, did they receive medical treatment while in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I think this question is very important and very complex, I would say. Officially, there was a male nurse supposed to be in charge of us, and his name was Gojko Jokanovic. He was a retired employee of the KP Dom, a male nurse. He had been brought from Montenegro to work there. He was in charge of us; that's what he had told me. However, I believe that although he wished to help us and he knew most of the prisoners, he didn't do their openly -- he didn't dare do that openly. He was afraid to, and he wasn't allowed to. I discussed this with him several times, and so did other inmates, and what he told us was that he could have problems if he helped us because the administration did not allow him to help us. Of course, we made do in various ways. There were so-called medical examinations, medical checkups for which we applied. Mostly us doctors and nurses and medical technicians applied for them as well as some other prisoners. And when we would come to the infirmary, we would steal medicines and other material from Gojko. Sometimes he would notice; sometimes he wouldn't. And I think that in a conversation we had, Dr. Torlak, myself, and others, we had agreed to save some medication for emergencies, especially for prisoner FWS-146 who had a bad asthma and couldn't live without medication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Gojko Jokanovic told you that he was not allowed by the administration to actually help you more than he would like to have done. Did he specify who in the administration did not allow him to do what he wanted?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't say that in so many words. He just said that those from the administration did not allow him to help us more, but he didn't name any names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he tell you what he feared would happen if he did not follow these orders? Did he indicate what would happen to him?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: He just said that he could have serious problems if he were to be caught helping us. He said, "I could have bad, awful problems."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, besides stealing, stealing medication, did you or other detainees get hold of medicines in other ways?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no other way there. It was possible for somebody from outside, somebody from a working group to bring in some medicines, but I don't believe that was the most important channel. I think it was rather our ability to make do in those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Gojko Jankovic. Did any medical doctors visit the KP Dom and treat detainees? Do you recall anybody?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: His name is Gojko Jokanovic, not Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, some doctors would come, even a dentist. He stayed for about a month, and later I saw him carrying a sackful of medicines and escorted by a guard. I saw him leaving the KP Dom and he never came back. In the beginning also a colleague of mine, a gynaecologist, Cedo Dragovic, used to come. I met him once. There was also the ear, throat, and nose specialist, Drago Vladicic. I never met with him there. And on one occasion I saw Dr. Reljo Divjan who just entered the building where the infirmary was located - he was wearing a military uniform - but he left very quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us try to specify the times when these doctors came. You said there was a dentist who came for about a month. Do you know which month?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: That was very early into the existence of the camp. It could have been the month of June, for instance. After June I never saw him there. He didn't show up. I heard he had fled for Belgrade. It was -- so he appeared for the first time in early June, and he was there for the entire month of June. As for Cedo Dragovic, I think he used to come the first three months, and perhaps sometime in September he disappeared as well. At least, he didn't come any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Drago Vladicic, when did he treat detainees?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: He took over from Dr. Cedo Dragovic, but I don't think he stayed long, either. He could have been there for about three or four months, perhaps, not longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that Mr. -- Dr. Reljo Div --

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Divjan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Divjan, yes. That he also came only once, and when was that; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: That was already 1993, maybe the summer of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When these various doctors came in the first month, did they come on a daily basis or less frequent?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I think they came only once a week.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they treat all the detainees that actually needed treatment, or what did they do?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I met up with Cedo Dragovic once. He wasn't examining any prisoners. There was a queue, and he was standing -- sitting at a desk. There was a guard there. He would ask the inmate, "What's wrong with you? What do you need?" But he didn't examine them. And since Gojko was always present there as a male nurse, he would give Gojko instructions as to whether to issue medicines or not. I think that they tried, within certain limits, to help the detainees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described to us the conversations you had with Mr. Jokanovic. I forgot to ask you: When did you discuss with Mr. Jokanovic, his possibilities to help? When was that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: That was not only once. We were exerting constant pressure to try to get them to improve the quality of treatment, especially for elderly people because we knew that the elderly were in greatest need of medical help. Myself and other doctors tried to get him to help us more and to get him to do certain things on the sly. We had not only one conversation with him. We talked to him whenever we could. We tried to find ways and means for him to procure medication and bring it in, and he would often do that. Sometimes he would show up in one of our rooms. He came to my room two or three times. He would call one of us out and give us some medicines so that the others don't see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us a time frame when these conversations with Gojko Jokanovic took place? Over your entire time of detention or when?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: If you mean this direct contact, when he told us that he couldn't help us more because administration did not allow it, that could have been in the beginning, in the early days of the camp, perhaps the first five or six months. If you mean that specific reply, that was in the fifth or sixth month into the existence of the camp. But I repeat: For the entire duration of our detention, we were constantly trying to get more than he could provide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Besides the rooms where detainees were detained, were there also some of them kept in isolation cells or solitary confinement?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were solitary cells. That's what we called them. They were on the ground floor of the left wing building, and they were located near the entrance to the KP Dom, on the right-hand side. I believe two solitary cells were on the right-hand side from the entrance, and I believe there was a total of four or five of them on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think I have to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness the photos 7512 and 7513. They are on the same sheet, one above the other. First this one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please have a look at the bottom photo first. Could you point out -- you said they were in the left -- they were in the left wing, and I -- no. Let's look at the top photo first. You said they were in the left wing, the isolation cells. Can you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. point them out here on this photo?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: It's not on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you call the left wing and the right wing? Maybe we can try to find out. Building 1, with this yellow number 1, that the left wing?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: No. I call it the right wing. Perhaps I'm wrong, but that's how I'm referring to it. To me, that is the right wing. The left wing is on the opposite side, completely elsewhere. On this side, there were no solitary cells at all. In buildings 1 and 2, there were no solitary confinement cells, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, the witness is obviously talking about his own perspective from inside the building. But so that we don't get any confusion later, perhaps if you could both refer to the wings as number 1 and number 2 even though it might cause a little problem for the doctor. Otherwise, we're going to be hopelessly confused when we read the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The building 2 -- you know, the building you see on this photo, there is a yellow number 2. Is that the building you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Number 2 is his left wing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your left wing. Would you call the building 2 the left wing?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: You asked me about solitary cells. The building 2 has no solitary cells. I can call it the central building. And the attachment, the annex, which is not visible here - it's a totally different building - this annex is what I'm calling the left wing. Perhaps we should call it building 3. Perhaps that's easier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Look at the bottom photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no. I think the best thing to do is to show him the plan because, you see, we have been referring to them as two separate buildings, number 1 and number 2, in effect. What he is saying is that what we call number 2, the jutting-out part, is a separate building, and what we see to the right of it, which is shown as number 3 in the bottom photograph, we've been calling that all part of building 2. So we're going to have to agree very clearly at the outset what it is we want to refer to. Now that I see that photo with the number 3 on it, I think the doctor is correct. Let's call that number 3 for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you see now the bottom photo, and there is a yellow number 3, would that be the section where the solitary cells were?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. We have clarified the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many detainees were kept in those solitary cells?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I think the exact number of detainees who passed through the solitary cells will never be known. We tried to count the meals that were carried to the detainees in those solitary cells and to calculate how many of them there were. We imagined if one meal was on the tray, there was one. If there were five meals, there were five people detained there. But the prison is structured in such a way that you can always, at any time, see what's going on within the compound, and nobody can enter without being seen by the administration and the prisoners because everything is centralised. Everything is in the field of vision. And because there are these solitary cells in building 3 and cells, solitary cells, in the administration building, we could judge by the number of meals how many detainees were kept there; but we could not know that during the night whether they were bringing somebody into those solitary cells, for instance, into the ones near the gate. So I don't believe it's possible to determine the exact number of people in solitary cells. We who were detained cannot claim with any degree of certainty what the number was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you yourself ever taken to a solitary confinement cell during your detention?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I was in a solitary cell only once, and that was a cell in building 3. I don't know the number of the room. They were numbered 1, 2, 3, and so on. I think the room I was in was number 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when were you taken there? When were you there?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: It was winter. It was January or February 1993. I think it was January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why were you taken there? What caused it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Since it was cold, we were trying to make some clothing out of blankets that a group found on the upper floors of building 3. We started making scarves, socks, vests, caps, to keep warm. And a large number of prisoners were involved, including myself. And one evening the guards burst in and confiscated everything, the blankets and what we had made already. Anyone who had this sort of makeshift clothing was taken to a solitary cell, and I was taken there for a pair of socks that I had made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long were you kept there?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I only spent the night there. I was released the next day. It wasn't long. I believe that one of the guards interceded in my behalf to let me out early.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who actually sent you into the solitary confinement? Who made this decision, do you know?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but the guard who had come, his name was Micevic and he was a neighbour of mine, he was the one who took me to the solitary cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you mistreated, beaten, or humiliated while you were in the isolation -- solitary confinement cell?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And any of the others that were also locked up there? I mean, while you were there, could you tell?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: At the time when I was there, I did not hear any voices or any sounds that would indicate that somebody was being abused, mistreated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in the solitary confinement cell, how did you feel? What did you -- yes, how did you feel?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I must say, I felt very miserable. The solitary cell is very narrow. The windows facing the street were on the wall. It was very cold. I had no blankets. I tried to pull up my knees and keep my -- keep warm, but the only way to keep warm is to keep pacing, so that's what I did. I paced from one corner of the solitary cell to the other, back and forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you afraid while you were in the cell?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Of course I was. I was frightened. I was alone, and I was afraid of the coming nightfall because I knew that ugly things could happen. I was actually expecting somebody to visit me that night, and I was prepared for a beating. I knew that anything could happen. However, nothing happened and no one came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you expect beatings or a visitor coming to your cell and doing bad things to you? Why did you feel that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Because during my stay in Room 16 and Room 18, I saw all these men who had been in solitary confinement cells and they talked about their horrible experiences from the solitary confinement cells, these guards and soldiers who came to beat them. Sometimes they were drunk; on other occasions they were not. However, at first in the months of June, July, May, I heard cries and screams of people from these isolation cells, and I expected something similar to happen to me as well, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your being taken there into the solitary confinement cell, was it a kind of punishment for having made the socks?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Exactly. I think that is quite correct because people were taken to solitary confinement for very plain reasons. If they would catch you playing cards, if they caught you heating water with a heater if you had one, if you did not observe the rules of conduct as they called them, you could be taken to solitary confinement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever punished for having violated the rules on another occasion?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I was punished because I made a mistake. Let's call it a mistake. Again, I trusted a Serb neighbour. Serb prisoners were right next door to us, so we could communicate through the door. Then in the anteroom of their room they had put a table where they placed bread, slices of bread. Our door, our door was ajar, and we saw some bread there on the table. Some of them would get into that room and take some bread, and then they would be beaten for it. Once I saw a Serb neighbour of mine, and he waved his hand at me, sort of telling me to get into that room and to get some bread, and then I was beaten for two or three minutes after he had beckoned me. A group of Serb soldiers was beating me on the head, although I tried to protect my head, and all over my body. I did manage to take the bread though. Then I went for an interview, as they called it, with Savo Todovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you here. You said a group of Serb soldiers were beating you on the head. Where did they come from? Were they in the building, in the prisoners' building?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: A group of Serb prisoners. These were prisoners who had violated the rules of the army of Republika Srpska, who did not want to fight or who had done something bad, who had stolen something or killed someone. They were imprisoned there in that room next door to us, so between us was only a small hall. So that's how we managed to communicate with them. They were not armed soldiers. They were prisoners at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you speak about your room, do you refer to Room 16?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: No. No. At that moment, I was in Room 18.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And when did this happen?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: That was the winter of 1993, the winter of 1993. I can't remember exactly. I can't remember the date, not even the month, but it was cold. It was wintertime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you had a kind of an interview with Savo Todovic. Can you describe where you had this interview and what was said?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: At the entrance into the building, into building 3, there is a small guards' room where the guards spend the night. It's a small room, perhaps 2 by 3 metres, perhaps even less than that. The guards took me to that room. Savo Todovic came and then he talked to me. I had expected him to punish me, to lock me up. However, he talked about my brother because he knew my brother very well. He said that my brother was a supporter of the Ustasha movement, that he was in Sarajevo at that time. Of course, that was senseless. I told him that I knew otherwise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he punish you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: It's very interesting. He did not punish me. That is very interesting. Of course I expected to be placed in solitary confinement on account of that. However, he did not do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he do?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: What he did really surprised me. He took me to the kitchen. He gave me a big dish with beans, and I practically ate all of it. After that, the guard returned me to the room. I don't know. I find that act quite inexplicable on his part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why? Did he usually treat detainees otherwise?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I think that as far as detainees are concerned, he was the one who was in charge. He's the one who said who would be taken to an isolation cell; who would be beaten; who would be going to the working group; who would be allowed to go outside the compound, who would not; who could be in which room, who could not. As far as the detainees themselves were concerned, he is the one who really determined their fate. He spent most of his time going to see the detainees, sending some detainees from certain rooms to other rooms. So I was afraid that he would put me in solitary confinement or that even worse things would be done to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already mentioned the Serb prisoners that were detained in the KP Dom. How many of them were there? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Sometime in March 1993, the prison in Foca admitted a group of them. Perhaps there was 100 of them or 80. Between 80 and 100. These were Serb prisoners who were transferred from the prisons of Republika Srpska or Eastern Herzegovina, Bileca, Gacko, Trebinje. So in March 1993, this number of Serbs was about 100. I think at that time, the Foca prison was their central prison, that it had that particular role or perhaps the role of a military prison because most of the Serb prisoners who were brought there were in military uniforms. Most of them had probably violated some military laws.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before March 1993, especially in summer or into your first month of detention, how many Serbs were there? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: That number could have been between 20, 30. Not more than that. I knew some of them. I knew that some of them were in the prison from the prewar days. They were in prison before the war. They worked in the kitchen, in the prison, within the prison compound. Of course, they were not locked up. They could go out, walk about. They had as much food as they wanted. They worked in the kitchen. They did things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, were there also soldiers among the Serb detainees?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I think there were deserters who had deserted from the front line, who didn't want to fight. I know that Simo Mojevic came then. I know him. He was my teacher. Boro Ivanovic, who went to see their soldiers and who gave them lectures, who tried to boost their morale, telling them that they had to fight, that that was the only way to resolve things, things like that. Then Suma was also detained for a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us return to Boro Ivanovic. Who was he? In relation to the prison, who was he? What was he doing there?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I had the opportunity of seeing him twice in the prison, I think. Once, I was listening. I was eavesdropping through the door. I think this was an action that was supposed to be taken by Serb soldiers in the area of Preljuca, perhaps. They didn't want to do that, and a lot of them were brought in, about 30. They were in military uniform. I knew some of them. They were my neighbours. They were brought there and put into a room. At that time, I was in Room 18, so I could communicate with them because there was this corner where they were put up. So practically, they were only two or three metres away from us, so we could communicate with them. One of them was from Ustikolina, and he told me that they had deserted, that they didn't want to fight. That night, Boro Ivanovic or Ivanovic, Ivanovic, he came in military uniform. I personally heard him attack them verbally saying, why did they desert? Why did they not want to fight the balijas? He was explaining the goals of the Serb struggle, explaining their objectives. That was it. I think he was a member of the military. I don't think he belonged to the KP Dom. That's my opinion. Let's say that he had some kind of military/political post, or that he was involved in educating the military or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On which facts do you base this opinion about his position?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Because I think he was not in the hierarchy of the KP Dom. I did not see him that often in the KP Dom. He was in military uniform. He had a small bag that usually political commissars carried in the Second World War. I heard what he was saying. I think that he did not have any direct link to us whatsoever, that he was only in charge of these Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said you saw him twice and you have already described the one incident. I forgot to ask you, when did this happen that you saw him making this speech to the deserters, when approximately?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: This was the autumn of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the second time that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly when this was. I think that at that time he was in the compound. He didn't enter the building. He was in the compound. He probably went to the administration building. I don't know. I don't know why he came, though, and he didn't stay for long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On this occasion, did he also speak with the Serb prisoners?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether he did then. I can't remember. Possibly so, but I can't remember. Although he entered the building to talk to Serb prisoners, I can't be sure. I cannot state with certainty that he entered the building, but he was in the compound, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw, when you saw Mr. Ivanovic entering the prisoners' building and speaking to the Serbs, was Mr. Krnojelac with him?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was anyone else from the prison staff with him, or was he able to enter the building alone, on his own?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: There had to be guards there to open the door for him. I think that some of the guards had to be with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you saw him in the compound on this other occasion, who was with him; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I think it was Savo Todovic, nicknamed Bunda.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Berberkic, we do not want to talk about the living conditions because other detainees have already told us all the details, and we do not have to repeat this. What I would like to know from you in this regard is only, did the living conditions, especially the lack of food, affect your physical health, and if so, in which way?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I weighed 87 kilos when I came to the camp. At one point I weighed 62 kilograms. I could not sleep well because my bones were aching. I had to find the right position. I had terrible problems. I vomited several times because of the stomach trouble I had. The weight loss probably led to some other reactions in my organism, so I had these terrible vomiting spells two or three times. I also had problems with my eyesight, probably due to a lack of vitamins. I saw things only dimly; I would not see clearly. I could hardly stand on my feet. Once I almost fell. I did not fall, but I almost fell, although a lot of people were falling around me, many of them due to exhaustion and a drop in blood sugar and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What affect did the living condition, especially the lack of food, have on the older or weaker detainees, besides the weight loss, of course?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: The elderly people who were there simply could not move about. They could not walk. They mostly lay down. If they would try to get up, they would fall. We explained to them that they had to try to get up gradually. And these signs of malnutrition were there, swellings on the feet and hands. Also due to lack of proteins, their skin was getting dry and parched. Hair was falling out. I think that all the classical forms of malnutrition were present. At one point, even lice appeared in Room 16 where I was, although we tried to keep the level of hygiene at a maximum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see food being delivered to the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Of course I did. In building 2 there was a warehouse. I think it's building 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, just to confirm, would the witness be shown the photo 7512. This one, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see there this building with the number "2" --

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's building 2, yes, yes. Down here on the ground floor where there are three windows, there's a door as well where there was a warehouse where even some of our people from the work group would unload cans with food and other types of food. Once I saw through the open door what was inside. That was the place. It was practically their warehouse, their storage room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness was indicating the basement with the door, that's the only door on this -- in this photo. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of food did you see? What kind of food did you see being delivered or stored in this storage room?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Most of it was canned food. And I think there was macaroni, rice, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the detainees receive this food?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then who used it? Could you see?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: That food was used, I think, by the Serb prisoners who were there and also the KP Dom staff. At first, when the KP Dom was established, that is, in June or July, the central mess where we ate was the central mess for the staff of the KP Dom, that is to say, for guards, for the management of the KP Dom and for the Serb prisoners as well. So they were the ones who used that food. We only found leftovers from these tins in the garbage and also leftover bread, leftover bread. Some people even rummaged through the garbage to find food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone die due to the living conditions? Not the beatings. I'm not -- we'll talk about beatings later on. Did anyone die due to the living conditions?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Due to direct consequences of starvation, no. I don't think that anyone died in the KP Dom as a direct consequence of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And indirect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's a very open-ended question, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. You're right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about the people who actually died. Do you know an Esad Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I knew Esad Hadzic from before. I was watching when one day - I think it could have been June - when they carried him out of the room, wrapped in a blanket. Later on, I communicated with Dr. Torlak over the window, and he told me that Esad's ulcer had perforated, that he requested him to be transferred to hospital urgently in order to undergo surgery. However, he said that the guards that were on night duty that night did not allow that to happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as I hear now, he was not in your room, Esad Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: No, he was not in my room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do not need to go into any more details except for you said "in June." Is it 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll take the adjournment now. We'll try to live by this crazy clock in this courtroom and resume at 11.30, according to that clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, before the break we spoke about some people who died in the KP Dom. I would like to know from you if you know a detainee Ibrahim Sandal.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I know Ibrahim Sandal. He was in my room, Room 18. I was with him for a while. He was very gravely ill. He couldn't move. He had lost his appetite. He couldn't eat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of an illness did he have?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I think he had heart trouble, high blood pressure, swollen legs. It must have been cardiac insufficiency or something like that. I don't know how he ended up in the KP Dom because I had left the KP Dom earlier. I later heard that he died there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know him from before the war?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this person beaten in the KP Dom or did he have signs of beating on his body?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: That was not my impression.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, this person is listed under 5.25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Berberkic, do you know a person with the name Omer Kunovac?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I know that person very well. He was brought into my room sometime in late May 1993. At that time, I was in building 3, on one of the upper floors. We were isolated, 12 of us detainees, when he was brought in, carried in because he couldn't walk. He was a deaf and mute person from Ustikolina. I hadn't known him. I had just heard about him. He couldn't talk. He was very badly beaten up. He had terrible stomach pains. He couldn't eat. And I was present when he died. I think he died on the 21st of June, 1993, sometime in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what caused his death?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I am absolutely certain that the cause of his death is an injury to the stomach caused by a blow, a blunt blow, a blow with a blunt object which caused injury to the stomach.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where he was beaten or who beat him?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: He had been beaten in a solitary cell in the administrative building. I don't know which cell, 1 or 2. I discussed him with Gojko Jokanovic. We asked Gojko Jokanovic that he be transferred to a hospital, and Gojko Jokanovic said it was out of the question. And when I said the man would die very soon and when I asked about what caused his injuries, he replied that it was Burilo's handiwork.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was it out of the question to bring him to the hospital? Did Gojko indicate why it was out of the question?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: No, no, he didn't say that. He didn't want to talk about that possibility at all. I think that Gojko was having problems with the administration right at that time because of the way he was helping us. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. It was obvious that he was being followed and that the carpet was being pulled from under his feet, and he was in danger, and it was obvious that he didn't want to discuss the possibility at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Kunovac was beaten in the isolation cells in the administration building. How do you know that? Did you hear anything, or was Kunovac himself indicated -- indicating this? How do you know?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: He didn't say anything because he couldn't talk. He was deaf and mute. He could just utter unintelligible sounds. He was carried in from the direction of the entrance from the administrative building. I don't know whether he had been in a solitary cell. Probably. But he was carried in from the administrative building which means that he hadn't been in the prisoners' quarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you said he was beaten in the isolation cells in the administration building, that is then your conclusion or your assumption?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I suppose that was it because that was the only place where it could have happened. I do not rule out the possibility that he was beaten up on the way to the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much time lay between him arriving in your room and his death? Could you say how many days?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Three weeks, approximately. I have already said that he was brought sometime in late May, and this was the 21st of June, so it was three weeks on the outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said according to what you saw, it was -- he was -- had a stomach injury caused by a blunt object, beating with a blunt object. What did you see that you came to this conclusion? What did you see on his body?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: At that moment Aziz Torlak was in the room, and we saw bruises on his stomach. It was a haematoma, an inside bleeding. I discussed this with Torlak because he knew more about it than I did, and he said it was probably an internal injury, an injury to an internal organ which required immediate intervention. Based on the appearance of his skin, the haematoma, the changes in colour, and the rigidity of the stomach, Torlak concluded that it was an injury to internal organs of the abdomen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this person is mentioned on Schedule B under number 35, and he is also mentioned under D-17; however, on D-17, his name is misspelled. It says "Omer Kukovac," but according to the dates and what is found out on the schedule, it has to be the same person; at least, that is what the Prosecution believes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Believes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you yourself beaten while you were detained in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I was beaten once in the KP Dom, and that happened not inside a building but in the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did it happen?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date. It could have been the autumn of 1992, but I cannot remember the exact date. However, I know how it happened, and I can describe it in detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: We were coming back from the canteen where we had had lunch. I was the last in the line. In front of me there was Dzevad Lojo, the manager of the mine. I was climbing down the stairs. I noticed that all the prisoners were sitting with their heads bowed. I didn't know what was happening. I heard this voice saying, "Bend your head. Bow." I didn't do that immediately. I wanted to see who was speaking. I think Dzevad Lojo didn't obey straight away either. Two soldiers in uniform, two armed soldiers, were there. I don't believe they were from Foca. One of them had a hat on his head. They had automatic rifles. They wore uniforms, camouflage uniforms. Dzevad Lojo received several blows and so did I. After that, of course, we had to bow, and with our heads bowed, we filed into our room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the two of you the only ones beaten on this occasion, Dzevad Lojo and you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, it was only the two of us, no one else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sustain any injuries?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: No, but I felt pain from a blow above my right ear, but there was no bleeding, there was just a swelling and bruises which appeared later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the soldiers or at least one of them wore a hat. What kind of a hat did he wear? Was it a usual soldier's cap or what was it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: It was a very unusual hat which I hadn't seen before. I think it was part of a camouflage uniform, but it was unusually large, something like a Mexican sombrero.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the soldiers spoke, could you hear any accent?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, could. I tried to see who they were. I saw one of them, and I don't think they were from Foca. I even think they were not from Serbia either, from somewhere around, perhaps. I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From their accent could you distinguish from where they could have been?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I believe they were from Eastern Herzegovina. I don't know exactly which place, but it could have been Bileca or Gacko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why these soldiers were in the compound?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I don't know the reason for their visits. Perhaps they had been there to have lunch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were guards present from the usual KP Dom staff? Were guards present when that happened?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was Milovan Vukovic from Josanica. He's a neighbour of mine and I know him. At first he didn't react. He must have been frightened too. All I know is he said, "Don't lift your heads. Don't look up."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the guard or the guards that were present, did they intervene while you were beaten?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't. Nobody intervened.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has just described the incident 5.12 in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did soldiers have access to the KP Dom in general?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I think that in the first few months soldiers could enter the KP Dom. Sometime in mid-June, a soldier wearing a uniform suddenly burst into Room 16. He wasn't armed. We were very much taken aback and frightened, but that soldier just entered the room, took it all in. He stayed for about ten seconds. He didn't say a word. He looked at all of us. He was probably looking for someone, but I don't think I had ever seen him in Foca. He was wearing a military uniform. Judging by his uniform, I believe he was a member of a paramilitary formation. He was obviously looking for someone specific, but he didn't utter a word, which surprised us. Ten seconds or so later, he left the room. In general, in the beginning, armed soldiers could enter the compound and our rooms, but that stopped happening later [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could they enter the room without guards? Could they simply go into the buildings where the prisoners were without any guard being present?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: No, they couldn't. The rooms were locked and the keys were kept by guards. So they couldn't come in on their own. One of the guards had to open the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you described this incident with the one soldier who burst into your room, and you said it was in mid-June. Is that mid-June 1992?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said after some time it stopped, this coming of soldiers stopped. When -- from when, what time onwards didn't soldiers come?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. With your leave, I have an objection. I didn't want to interrupt earlier. It says in the transcript that it stopped happening. What he actually said was that it happened less often. And my learned friend asked this question because I had failed to react before. Perhaps it would be a good time to clarify now that the witness actually said that that happened less often. It says it stopped happening in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: At line 12, "... but that stopped happening later," yes. Well, if there's some problem, if there's some problem just ask the question. I was not pausing in order to remember your name, Mr. Bakrac. I was trying to find the button to turn my microphone on which was covered by a book. I'm sorry about that. Anyway, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, you ask the question again, see what the answer is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did soldiers come into the compound throughout your detention, or did it stop at one point in time?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I think it stopped at some point, and I think that point was after the New Year 1993. From then on there were no more entries by armed soldiers into the prisoners' quarters or the compound. But in the first five or six months that used to happen, soldiers would come into the compound and into our rooms; but later that stopped. I don't know if you are now satisfied with my answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just -- I also forgot to tell you that the guard that was mentioned being present during the beating of this witness is actually mentioned in P-3 under the number 45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you interrogated while you were in the prison?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I was interrogated in June, I believe it was. I believe it was the 23rd of June. One of the guards came to fetch me, took me to the administrative building and ushered me into one of the rooms on the first floor. Maybe it was the second floor. Yes, I believe it was the second floor. He ushered me into a room where Zoran Vladicic, an investigator, was sitting behind a desk. I knew him from before, and we even cooperated on business. We even cooperated on certain cases before the war. And there was also in that room one person wearing a military uniform. His trousers were olive grey, and he wore a black T-shirt. That person kept silent all the time during my interrogation. He was just present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that it was on the 23rd of June. What year?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Zoran Vladicic you said, an investigator, investigator at that time or even before? Where did he work and what did he do before the war?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was an investigator even before the war. I worked in the admissions section in the infirmary of the hospital, and whenever an accident happened, he would show up. I believe he was an investigator with the SUP of Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said you were interrogated in an office on the second floor in the administration building. Entering the investigation -- the administration building through this metal door, had you to turn to the right or to the left part of the administration building?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: To the right. We went to the right part of the administration building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And what were you questioned about during this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I first spent some time waiting in the hallway, and there was another prisoner with me waiting to be interrogated. His name was Sisic. I don't know his first name. He was from Ustikolina, 20-ish. And FWS-162 was interrogated before me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mean on the same day?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, the same day. Zoran Vladicic asked me how I had been wounded, what had been happening to me, whether I had any weapons. I told him that a bullet was taken out of my body in the hospital, that I was not wounded in combat, that I was hit by a shrapnel. I thought -- he insinuated that I was wounded in combat. I said that was absolutely not true, that it was nonsense. He had inquired about who had distributed weapons to Muslims, who had weapons, who was a member of the SDA. I denied everything. I had no knowledge of that at all. I simply wasn't interested. And he told me that I belonged to a group of doctors who wanted to organise themselves to poison Serbian children and patients in hospitals, and that allegedly in a family house in Foca -- in my family house in Foca they found a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. machine-gun. I denied all that. Then he asked me whether I had voted for a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina. I replied yes. He asked me whether I had attended political rallies in Foca. I said I had attended only one rally in the school centre. He took out from his drawer a file, and he told me that I was telling the truth, that he knew everything, that he had all the data there, that he knew which rally I had attended, he knew who I consorted with, who my friends were, but there was a way to make me confess what he wanted to know. And he said it was better for me to confess than for him to send me to "the basement," as he put it. And he also said, "Anything can happen during the night." I told him then that I could not confess to what I hadn't done, especially not poisoning of Serbian patients who had been wounded or Serbian children. He knew me from before, and he knew my family. He put a paper in front of me which I was supposed to sign. I read what was written there. I saw that it wasn't written anywhere -- that nothing about poisoning was written there on that paper, and I signed the paper. Then I was taken back to my room, Room 16.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The accusations like having a machine-gun in your home, were they true or false? Did you have a machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Of course they were false.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that he indicated "the basement," that you would be taken to the basement and a lot of things could happen. What did that mean? Did you know what he was talking about?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I think that he was quite direct. He said that there was this basement and that during the night all sorts of things could happen, that the soldiers would visit me. That's the way he put it, that the soldiers would visit me, and, "You know what that means." That's what he said to me. Detainees who were interrogated before I was, some of them returned to the room after being taken out while others were taken to this basement and kept there for a night or two or three. I don't know how long. That was probably one of the ways of making people confess what they were being asked to confess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were interrogated, and you mentioned already this Mr. Sisic, did you hear anybody being beaten or shouted at in the other offices?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Then, in those offices, I did not hear anyone being beaten, no. I know that Witness FWS-162 cried for a long time, that he was defending himself, saying that he was not what they were saying he was. I know that he was crying out loud. As for Sisic, I don't think that he was beaten then at all. Actually, I'm sure that they didn't beat anyone while I was there in those offices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned already that you saw persons return to your room with injuries or with signs of beating. Can you tell us whom you recall who came back with the signs of beating?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I remember three detainees very well. The first detainee who was taken out that day was my brother-in-law, Nedzad Delic, who was in Room 18, above me. He was taken to the gate. One of the guards took him to the gate. I heard moans, cries, his screams, him beseeching them. He's a young man, about 20 years old, very tall and strong. He was there for about half an hour. I was watching through the window of Room 16. When the gate opened, two guards carried him into the compound. He could not walk. They were holding him on the sides. He had been beaten up. They returned him to Room 18. After that, I found out that he could not stand on his own feet for a few days and could not walk for a few days. Immediately after him, Emir Mandzo was taken out. He was in Room 16 together with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just stop you here and ask you a few more details. When did this happen? Do you recall when Mr. Delic was taken?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: It could have been the month of July, mid-July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what time of the day?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: The afternoon, the afternoon. Well, the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The early afternoon or the late afternoon, if you know?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I think it was after lunch; that is to say, it could have been around 2.00 or 3.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said mid-July. Is it 1992 or later?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that you heard afterwards the sounds of beating. Could you recognise his voice? Screaming, sorry.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Of course I could. He's my wife's brother, and there's no doubt in my mind that it could have been somebody else's voice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you recognise the voice of the people who did that to him?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I met up with him after that, perhaps about a month later, in the mess. It just so happens that his room and mine were having lunch at the same time. I talked to him very briefly. He said that his schoolmates had beat him, or neighbours. He said that Zoran Matovic, a guard who is from Josanica and who was a guard at the KP Dom who guarded us there, was off that day. It was not his shift. He was not working a shift on that day. He brought a group from the town of Foca, including his schoolmates and neighbours, including Zoran Vukovic, who was a karate man, and then he described to me how they had beat him. He told me that while we were in the canteen. He said that when they brought him into that room, that they put a tarpaulin over his head and that they beat him with their hands, they kicked him, that he fainted a few times, that they splashed water on him.
