When he came to, he realised that they had made a circle around him and that most of them were under the influence, that they had a bottle of brandy that was going round, that they were drinking, that they were drunk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he mention if Zoran Matovic was actually involved during the beating? Was he present during the beating? Did he mention anything like that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: He said that Zoran Matovic was present and that he brought that group from town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that you could hear the sounds, his screaming and the sounds of beating. From where did the sounds come, from where in the administration building? Could you locate that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: They came from the solitary confinement cells. I think this is the premises when you enter the KP Dom you go to the right-hand side, and there are two rooms there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness the Exhibit 6/1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, another detainee made this floor plan, and it is supposed to be the ground floor of the administration building that you see on the lower building indicated. Do you recognise it? Can you orient yourself? Can you show us where the entrance is that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you are actually referring to. Do you mean the entrance to the KP Dom from the outside --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: -- or the gate, the gate from the prison compound? What are you referring to actually?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said just a minute ago, you said right from the entrance, and I simply want to show -- you to show us what you meant with the pointer. There is a pointer on your desk, and you have to point it on the ELMO, not on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: This is where the entrance to the administration building is. Room 1 and Room 2 are the rooms where this happened, where the beatings took place, Room 1 and Room 2. I think it was Room 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has just pointed out the rooms -- soba 1 and soba 2 on the right side from the metal door.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And allowing for some, allowing for some delay with the translation, he was pointing to where everybody else has said is the door into the compound from the administration building as being such.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is there some problem with that, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, he pointed at the entrance into the administration building from the compound of the KP Dom, and he said that then you turn right. That's what he said. And this is left, what he showed now.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: No, no, please. I said quite clearly when I was being interrogated that I entered the gate and then I turned right. And now I know, of course, that when I enter the gate, the rooms are on the left. I mean, really, there is no confusion about this. No confusion whatsoever. But this is not right. The warehouse, the storage room, is not in the right place here. I think it's in the wrong place, or there is something missing here or number 1 is missing. I don't think this map is good, at least, not this upper part, the premises where we had been detained.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I can also -- to clarify the matter further, we can use a photo. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That would be better.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. With the help of the usher, I would like to show the photo 7477, this photo. It's the lower.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you would please look at the lower photo, and the rooms that you just mentioned, are they on the photo, at least, the windows?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, the windows of those rooms are on the photograph. When you enter the gate from the prison compound, they are on the left. There's no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you point at the windows with the pointer?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: It's the window here, the other window, and then the third window. Now, this could have happened: It could have been window number 2 or Room 1, whichever way you want to put it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the witness was indicating the three ground-floor windows left from the door, and he was especially indicating the second window from the left -- or from the right, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The middle window.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, thank you. In reference to the victim Nedzad Delic, it's the incident B-15. And the witness had also mentioned the guard Zoran Matovic involved, and that is the person P-48, on P-3, the person number 48.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just have another question. Nedzad Delic, does he have a nickname Stela, or is Stela Delic a different person?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Nedzad Delic has a nickname, but it's quite different from the one you mentioned. His nickname is Pico. I don't know who Stela is, though. I don't know about that at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. It was just a question. Did your brother-in-law, did he survive the KP Dom, or is he missing?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: No, he's registered as missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did he leave the KP Dom and how?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I think that could have been the month of September when he was taken out. He was taken in a group of some 30 men. All of them were young men from 20 to 35 years old. We were then told that they were being taken out to do some kind of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us the year?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: That was 1992. I do apologise. From now on I will really try to state the year when something happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said they were called, they were told -- you were told that they were being taken out to do some kind of work. What kind of work, do you know?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: We were not told then. Later when we talked to certain guards, we tried to find out a bit more. I asked one of the guards very directly - we were close - and I asked him what had happened to him and this entire group, actually. I said to him, "Is it possible that they went out to work?" And he said to me, very directly, that all of that was just talk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that your brother-in-law is still missing?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he is registered as missing. Of course, he's not alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that actually three people returned to your room or you saw being returned with injuries. Who is the second one? We have Delic, and now who is the second one that you remember?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: The second one, the second one was Hasan Dzano. He's also from Josanica. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise for interrupting, and I'm sure that this was done by my colleague inadvertently. It says in the transcript that Hasan Delic was returned to the witness's room. That's not what I understood the witness to say earlier on during his testimony, that Hasan Delic and two others returned to "his" room. That's what the transcript said. I think that before he did not say that Hasan Delic was returned to his room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not sure I see what the distinction is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness said he was in Room 18, he was above. He did not say he returned to his room. I did not follow the transcript. So there then should be a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But what is the distinction? He was returned to his own room or the witness's room, is that what the problem is? The word "his" there is ambiguous.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. In the transcript, I saw the question being put, saying that the Delic returned to his room. That's not what the witness said before. And even now my learned friend said that the witness had said that he had returned to Room 18, not 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you had better sort it out. As I read the transcript, it seems to me to be correct, but if there is a problem, please sort it out, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, your brother-in-law, in which room was he when this beating occurred?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I would have to say something. Please let me say something before that. There is no person called Hasan Delic. There is only Nedzad Delic. The gentleman said just now "Hasan Delic." There is no such person Hasan Delic. There is only Nedzad Delic. I said that quite clearly, and I said he was in Room 18 at that time and that he was taken out and that he was returned to Room 18. The other two detainees were with me in Room 16, and they bear the following names: Hasan Dzano and Emir Mandzo. That is the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Hasan Dzano, who was he? Did you know him from before?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was my neighbour. He was about 65 years old. He was a retiree from the village of Josanica. He had surrendered in Josanica, and he was taken to the KP Dom. He was taken out of my room. He was in the same room with me. He was taken out. He was beaten by the same group that beat my brother-in-law. He had a hat on his head then - I remember that - because he was a huntsman. He told me later, after he returned to my room, how he had been beaten. He was beaten in an identical way. First they took off his hat when they brought him in there, and then they said to him, "You're not going to go hunting deer in the forest any more. You'll never have an opportunity of being a huntsman again." They threw his hat away, they put a tarpaulin over his head, and they beat him. He kept falling. The guards also helped him get back to my room or, rather, carried him to my room. Of course I walked up to him straight away. His back was all black and blue. He had a laceration about ten centimetres long, and this was probably inflicted by a soldier's boot, underneath his left jaw, which was bleeding. He also had a footprint where his chest bone is, and the marks were quite clear. And he had problems with breathing. He could not breathe. We put some cold compresses on him immediately, salt as well. We did have some salt. I tried -- I tried to examine his chest, but I think that his chest bone was broken. I also sewed up his wound, the laceration that was bleeding. I used a needle and black thread. We also gave him a pain-killer. We had a pain-killer called Analgin. He could not walk. We brought his food to the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that he was beaten by the same group as your brother-in-law. Does that mean that he was taken on that same day to the administration building?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, the same day. He was taken out right after my brother-in-law. When my brother-in-law was returned to Room 18, the guard came to our room and took Hasan out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said what Hasan told you afterwards, but what did you yourself see and hear?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you're actually referring to. I described what I saw, what he looked like. I also heard cries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That's not what I was asking you. What did you hear when he was taken? Did you hear cries and blows?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I heard moans, cries. You know, when you're beating an old man -- when old men moan, then this is a special kind of moan, a special kind of cries. This was like screaming. He was beseeching them not to beat him. He probably was in terrible pain. He was very loud.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise his voice?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Of course I recognised his voice. That man was a neighbour of mine and we were friends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the sounds come from the same room that you indicated previously?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. No doubt about that. It was the same room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much time did Mr. Dzano need to recover from these injuries?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: He always had problems with his breathing. He could never breathe normally. He was in pain. The swellings on his back subsided over a few days. However, other swellings appeared. There were still bruises on his back, though, and he also had pain on both sides. The laceration had grown together though. He did not have any other problems, but he needed about seven days to come to, in a way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did Mr. Dzano leave the KP Dom? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. It could have been the month of September, the beginning of September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did he leave?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Quite simply, they came -- a guard came and called out a group, and his name was within this group. There was no explanation given, no nothing. These names were just called out. There was a list of people, and his name was on this list. He took his things and left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you speaking about the year 1992 again?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I am speaking about the year 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if he is still alive? Did you ever find out?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I think he's dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you think that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Because he never appeared anywhere. No one knows anything about him. I talked to his family after that. There's been no trace of him that could possibly lead to him being found.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just one more question in relation to him. Does he have the nickname Kalabic or something similar?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's his real nickname, Kalabic. A very interesting nickname, but that is his nickname.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the person we just spoke about is listed under B-18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the third person that you saw return with injuries into your room, who was that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: His name is Emir Mandzo. Of course I knew him. He worked at the Neurology Department of the Foca hospital. He got a son a month before the war, and he carried his picture around. He had his picture in the KP Dom. His wife gave birth a month before the KP Dom. He was taken out after Hasan Dzano. The guards took him out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that he is a young man?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: He could have been 22, 23.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And what did you see when he was taken out?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: He was taken to the gate and again screams and moans were heard, someone falling down from a chair. In prison, you develop new senses. I was in Room 16, and we heard every sound. You heard a blunt object falling. You heard water flowing, and he later told me how he had faired. It was the same group of people. They were, most of them, his neighbours. These three prisoners had been neighbours. He, too, was beaten by the same group of people. He told me how it was. They did not throw a tarpaulin over his head, they just started beating him. He fainted several times and even, as he later told me, he was near death for a while. He came to when they splashed water on him. They perched him up on a chair. Then they took another chair, they took off his shoes, they inserted his arms and legs through the frame of the other chair. One of them took a baton and beat him on the arms and legs. Zoran Vukovic, who was a karate man from Josanica, hit him with his soldier's boots on the jaw, and he fainted again. He says that he lost consciousness several times, then they splashed water on him and he would come round again, and all that could have lasted for half an hour, maybe more. Then they brought him back into the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear the sounds of beating and screaming again from that same room that you had previously shown to us?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, very clearly. It was not only myself who heard it, but all the prisoners who were inside. Some of them could not bear to listen. They put pillows on their head. We were terrified. We thought it would go on and on, and that it would end tragically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of injuries did you later see on Mr. Mandzo?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: His face was completely distorted from the blows. His upper lip was lacerated. His teeth were broken in the upper jaw. He had awfully large swellings on the soles of both his feet. He had swollen back sides the hands, and his index fingers were broken. His entire body was one huge wound. It was black and blue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much time did he need to recover or ...

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: He couldn't get up for about three days. We had to carry him. He was able to stand up later, but he was in great pain. But the swellings came back very soon. We had put cold water compresses on his arms and legs, and the swellings subsided. But for three days he couldn't eat and he couldn't get up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mandzo leave the KP Dom before you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: He was taken out of the KP Dom in the same group as Hasan Dzano, and nothing has been heard of him since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have contact with his family members as well, Mr. Mandzo's, I mean?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: No, I had no contact at all. I only heard that his wife had survived and that she was somewhere abroad together with his son.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This incident is listed, Your Honour, this incident is listed under B-37.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, these beatings that you just described, was this the only time this day, was it the only time that you heard the sound of beatings from this room that you showed us; or did you hear more similar sounds from this room on other occasions?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't the only time. I believe from the first half of June until the end of June there had been more. I think June was the most awful month. It was the time when prisoners were taken out to the gate or to those rooms and were abused and beaten there. The middle of June, the second half of June and the 28th of June, which was St. Vitus day, that was the period when we could clearly hear the screams, moans. We could hear people begging those who were beating them not to beat them. They were saying, "Please, please, don't. I haven't done anything."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are we talking about June 1992?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: It was June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we actually do not need to go into the general pattern in which those incidents occurred, but I would rather like to address with you particular victims that you had mentioned in previous statements that you gave to the Prosecutor's Office or to the Bosnian authorities. Do you know the Rikalo brothers or Rikalo relatives?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: They are Rikalo brothers, not relatives. I knew them well. Husein Rikalo is the eldest. He is my generation. Zaim Rikalo is younger, and Hidajet or Hido is the youngest. I knew all three of them well. They used to come to my house, and I believe they are even some distant relatives of mine. They were in the KP Dom, and they were said to have been brought there from Montenegro. In that month, all of those three men were taken out to the gate and were beaten, all three of them. And the eldest Rikalo was beaten up Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the worst, Husein Rikalo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that? Could you recognise his voice, or how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I know because I could clearly recognise his voice, and I know the exact words he was uttering. He was saying, "Please don't, please don't beat me. Please." And he repeated that three or four times, "Please don't beat me."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear when Husein was beaten, did you hear anything else besides his voice? Did you hear the voice of those who did this to him?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I heard voices, but I couldn't tell to whom they belonged. I heard them asking him, demanding something like, "Where did you bury it? Tell us. We'll kill you." I don't know what they meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were these three Rikalo brothers, were they in your room when they were taken, or if not, where were they?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: They were not in my room. I don't know the number of the room they were in. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they in the same building as you, or were they in the other building, in the building 1; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: They were in building 1, but I don't know which room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you see them go through the yard?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned Zaim, Husein -- Zaim Rikalo. Did you also recognise his voice when he was beaten, or was it only Husein that you recognised?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I recognised his voice, too. I can claim with absolute certainty about the two of them. I'm not sure about the youngest because I hadn't socialised with the youngest brother, but I'm sure about the elder two, and I know those were their voices. I can't be sure 100 per cent about the youngest brother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that the youngest brother's name was Hido. Do you know any Mithat Rikalo?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I don't know who that person is. It's not familiar to me at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you, did you see these Rikalo brothers taken only once, or were they taken several times for beatings?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I believe the eldest was taken out several times. I'm not sure about the other two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Husein? Did you see him, with injuries, return to his building?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes. After this happened, he never came back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was: You said that Husein was taken several times. Did you ever see him return? On any of these occasions, did you see him return with injuries?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I can't remember that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you ever hear or see them again after they were taken for the last time?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I have spoken to his mother in Sarajevo. She told me that she has some information to the effect that they had been killed, although she was hoping for a long time, and she searched for them for a long along time. She solicited the help of various organisations, but then she has lost all hope that they could be alive.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, the victims Rikalo brothers are listed under B-45 to 48 and C-21 to 23, although there is no Hido Rikalo listed but instead a Mithat Rikalo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To clarify this point further, can you tell us -- you said that Hido was the younger of the brothers. What was his job? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: No. No, I don't know what he did for a living.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he look like? Can you describe him?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: He was tall, thin, with short hair. He had a baby face, I would say, very clear complexion. His hair was brown and short.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Did you see that Nurko Nisic was taken?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what you saw and heard?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I saw Nurko Nisic more than once. I think he was taken out of his room more than once and returned. He had swellings, haematomas on his face. He had lost so much weight that I had trouble recognising him, although he had been my neighbour in Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in your room or where?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: No, he wasn't in my room. He was in building 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you see his injuries that you just described?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I was in Room 16 at the time, and the path the prisoners had to take from building 1 to the canteen was very close to my windows. The distance was less than two metres. So we could see everything from our windows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that he was taken on several occasions. In that time period that you mentioned, that is the second half of June 1992 or is it in a different time period?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: That was in June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said he was taken several times. Do you know how many times?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but I think it was more than five times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him being taken for the last time, did he return?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: He didn't return to the room then, but I heard the guards' voices. I heard the voices of the guards who were calling him. They were saying, "Nurko, Nurko."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you hear this, calling him "Nurko, Nurko."

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: That was in the second half of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From where did these voices come from when you heard this "Nurko, Nurko."

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: They came from Room 2, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean where the beatings occurred? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the room I mean, by the gate, inside the administrative building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you heard this calling "Nurko, Nurko," did you hear at the same time the sound of beatings?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could hear that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you recognise the voices of the guards that were calling out?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: No. I cannot be sure, but I think it was Dragan Obrenovic. However, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find out later on that he died or if he is still missing? Did you speak with his relatives?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I spoke to one of the guards in the prison who told me that Nurko had died during a beating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name of this guard or are you not willing to reveal his identity?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I would rather not, not yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Because he's in a position where he could have problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Bico Hamed, nicknamed Salem?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I forgot to give you the numbers. It's C-19 and 5.27 in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bico Salem or Hamed, do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I know him as Salem Bico. I know that he was a policeman in Foca, and I saw him in the KP Dom. He was in building 1. I saw him with swellings around his eye, and haematomas. He had obviously been beaten, and he is one of the group who was taken out in the second half of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you hear, if anything? Did you hear anything when he was taken out on these obviously at least two occasions?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I didn't know him well and I did not recognise his voice, so I cannot claim one way or the other with certainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But when he was taken, did you hear the sounds of beating at that same time?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I heard the sound of beating, but I didn't hear his voice nor would I have been able to recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this person is listed under C-2 and B-5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Halim Konjo. Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I know Halim Konjo. He was in the KP Dom. He's one of the group which was taken out in end June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he taken out only once or did you see him being taken on several occasions?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I think he was interrogated several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "interrogated," do you actually mean these beatings that you described to us or do you mean something else?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I think that in the beginning, we thought of that as interrogations and that is why I used this term. In the beginning, the guards, when they were taking out prisoners, they said it was for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll be adjourning until 2.20, I remind you, rather than 2.30, and we will adjourn this afternoon at 3.20. So until 2.20, according to the court clock. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all I would like to apologise to my learned friend for interrupting the continuation of her examination; however, I would like to clarify a matter that I believe is quite urgent. We got a message from a psychologist who we wanted to call as an expert, namely, Ms. Ana Najman does not now exactly how she is supposed to present her findings. Does she come to findings of her own and then send these findings to the representative of the OTP, or is she supposed to work together with a representative of the OTP, that is to say, the person who will be present during the examination of the accused? I've been asked by her to clarify this so that she could come to her findings as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: My understanding, and I'll check it with the Prosecution in a moment, is that there is a joint examination so that there can be discussion between the two experts, but each is expected to give an independent advice or opinion. Does that make it clear enough for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do you have anything to say, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we actually also thought it would be this way, and we actually were advised by our expert that they usually work in this way. The psychologist makes the tests in the presence of the psychiatrists, and the results of the tests is later on discussed with -- by both of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. They don't have to agree upon the results, but they should be there and the opportunity is there for them to discuss the matter with each other. If they come to an agreement, all the better; if they don't, it doesn't matter. We want independent reports anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I understood that. However, I'm interested in the written version. What should be presented in writing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Her own opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of one expert, you mean? Does our expert send his or her opinion to the expert of the Prosecutor, or do they work on this opinion together in writing and do they then defend it here, or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I thought I'd made it reasonably clear. It is open to them to discuss it amongst each other, and one would hope that they will. But each is responsible for writing his or her own report, and the other one may comment upon it, the first doctor's report, if they wish. But there is no suggestion that it has to be a joint report or that they have to be working together on each other's reports. They are independent reports, and they are independent opinions, but one hopes that they will discuss the matter before they come to their own opinions.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually our psychiatrist has informed us that he needs the results -- she needs the result of Mrs. Najman because the tests done by Ms. Najman are tests only conducted by psychologists. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And she needs the test results. She needs them for her report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Because she cannot conduct the tests herself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I thought that there may be the provision of reports at the time of the consultation, at least, the results of the testing; but if they haven't, then clearly the psychiatrist needs the psychologist's report. But what we are seeking to have from them is at least the opportunity for each to consider the other's opinions on the matter. But they are to be independent opinions expressed in the end. Now, does that make it clear?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And, Your Honour, for your information, the tests and also the discussion with the accused have already been conducted, and our expert said as soon as she has the results of the tests, she needs something like two or three days to make her own report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. And then she will give it to Miss or Mrs. Najman so she will have the opportunity of commenting on them as she wishes just as the psychiatrists will no doubt comment upon anything Ms. Najman produces.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Does that clear it up?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I think it's clear to me. I'm going to instruct our expert to write her own opinion and then to send that kind of report to the OTP or, rather, their expert. Then I expect the expert of the OTP to send his or her opinion to our expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Exactly. Right. Let's get on with the doctor's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I'm receiving a lot of noise. Do you also receive all this background ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We're not so fortunate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, before the break we spoke about Halim Konjo, and I would like to know from you --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise, but I can't hear my learned friend at all. I hear all sorts of voices and noise coming from some other room apparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are you using channel 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, somebody up in the control booth there can sort this one out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do you want something said as a test? Can you hear the translation now?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much for the assistance from the booth. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Berberkic, we spoke about Halim Konjo, and you mentioned that he was taken to the administration building on several occasions. Did you see him return on any of these occasions with injuries?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I saw him twice, I think, and he had bruises on his face. It looked like injuries sustained due to blows, that is to say, haematoma, swellings underneath the eyes, things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whenever he was taken in this time period, did you hear the sounds of the beating and screaming?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear that, but I cannot say for sure whose voice it was. I wasn't that close to him. I cannot say for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him for the last time being taken, did he disappear after that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: He's in that group of prisoners that was taken away around the end of June 1992. He never returned to the room. I have no information. I don't know what happened to him. I heard that some people from the work group allegedly saw his corpse in the hospital, in the morgue there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who from the work group? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: That was detainee FWS-210.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's C-13 and B-33 where this person is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kruno Marinovic. Do you know him and did you see him in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I did not know him personally from before, but my detainees showed me this person, told me who he was. He was also beaten several times. I saw him through the window. He was in Room 1 [sic]. His injuries were more or less similar to the injuries sustained by the other prisoners who were taken out at that time. His face was swollen, he had swellings, haematoma. Swellings around the eyes, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the last time that you saw him being taken, did he disappear as the others that we have mentioned before?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: He disappeared together with this group of people. He never, he never reappeared, never, since June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At least the translation that we got was that he was in Room 1. I suppose you mean building 1. Is that right, that he was in building 1?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I meant building 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this person is mentioned under C-17 and 5.27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zulfo Veiz, do you know him?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I know him well. He was a policeman in Foca. He belonged to this group of people. I saw him several times in the KP Dom. He was beaten several times, taken out to the gate. He had haematomas. I think that his right eye was almost closed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was he in the buildings?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Building 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this person is mentioned under C-29 and 5.27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Munib Veiz, do you know this person as well?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I know Munib Veiz from before. He was in camp in building 1. I think he was in a room on the first floor, but I'm not sure, but he was in building 1 for sure. I saw him a few times. He had lost lots of weight although he had spent only one month in prison. He was taken out several times for beatings. He wore a leather jacket since he worked in a shop that belonged to Visoko. He was selling leather goods as well. The last time he was taken out with a group of people, this was the end of June 1992. I remember the blows exactly, this characteristic sound when a baton hits leather. It's a soft sound but yet a reverberating sound when something hits leather. However, I didn't hear a word from him. He never returned again. I never saw him in prison since then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that you -- he was taken several times. Did you see him returning on these other occasions, when he returned, with injuries?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I saw him. I think he had injuries on his face and lips.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this person is mentioned under C-28 and B-59.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kemo Dzelilovic, do you know him?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I know Kemo Dzelilovic. He was in the KP Dom in building 1. He belongs to this group of people who went missing the end of June 1992. I did not notice any injuries on him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him being taken several times for beatings, or only that one time when he disappeared?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I think that he was not taken out several times. I think that he was taken out only once, that being the last time as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this person is mentioned under C-7 and B-19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kuloglija, Mustafa, did you see him in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I know him from before. He was at the KP Dom in building 1. He belonged to this group of people who had gone missing. I did not notice any signs of violence on him, at least, not that I can remember. I don't think he had been beaten several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say he belonged to the group that went missing in June, do you always refer to these people who were beaten and then disappeared? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I mean the group of people who were taken away in the interval between mid-June and the end of June 1992. I think that then the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters can no longer hear the witness, no sound whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We've lost the whole sound.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I am referring to the group of people who were taken away from mid-June 1992 until the end of June the same year, and I think that then about 40 persons were taken out of the camp. I tried to make a list, and I know about 37 people for sure, but I think that there were a few more.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after each of these people were taken, did you always hear the sound of beatings?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, these were sounds of beatings, mistreatment. However, I think that at the end of June - it could have been St. Vitus' Day, the 28th of June - I think I heard gunshots as well. Yes. Yes, I did hear gunshots then. The question is whether it was actually on the 28th or after that, but I do maintain it was the end of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But we were talking about several people. Up till now and whenever they were taken, including the last -- Mustafa Kuloglija, did you always hear the sound of beating?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mustafa Kuloglija is under C-15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Fuad Mandzo?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I know Fuad Mandzo. I think that he was captured as a fighting man somewhere around the hospital. He was beaten on several occasions, and he is also one of the persons belonging to that group that were taken out towards the end of June 1992. However, I cannot remember whether he had any injuries on his face or on his body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fuad Mandzo, how old was he and what was he doing? What was his job?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: He was born the same year I was, but I don't know what he was by profession. I know him. We were together at a federal work drive for young people many years ago, but I don't know what he actually did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did he live in Foca, in which neighbourhood? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I don't know where he lived, in which part of town.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the person C-16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Enes Uzunovic, was he in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Enes Uzunovic worked together with me in the hospital. I know him well. I think he was brought from the hospital to the KP Dom. He was beaten several times. He was taken out for interrogations as well. Signs of beatings and violence could be seen on him. I would say that these were standard injuries sustained by persons who were beaten, that is to say, swellings on their faces, eyes that were shut, haematoma. He is one of the people who went missing towards the end of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Uzunovic, in which room was he? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: He went out of building 1. I don't know exactly. Later, after he was taken out, through certain channels I got his coat. His coat was all bloody. I tried to wash the blood off the coat but I didn't manage to, and I tried several times. I simply wouldn't wash the blood off. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that it was his coat?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I know because I saw him wearing that coat. He had that coat in prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say through "channels" you got it, what kind of channels were that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Some of the prisoners who were in his room. I can't remember who exactly. He left that coat, actually. Then one of the prisoners, when he came to my room, he gave me the coat and said that it was his coat. Of course I recognised the coat too because several times I saw him go out in that coat. He wore that coat when he went to work in the hospital as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, its the person C-26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mate Ivancic. Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I know Mate Ivancic well. He worked at the ear, nose, and throat department in the Foca hospital. I think that he was also brought to the KP Dom from his working place. I saw him in the camp. I cannot confirm whether he was beaten or not. However, he was one of the people who were taken out towards the end of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he -- in which building was he detained?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I think that he was also in building 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's C-11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Meha Pasalic. Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I know a person called Mehmed Pasalic. It is probably one in the same person. His nickname was Meha. He had a private business of his own, a shop in a part of town called Cohodar Mahala. He was in building 1. He was also taken out of the KP Dom towards the end of June 1992. I think that he had been beaten and mistreated, but I can't remember what his face looked like. I cannot remember the injuries that he might have had.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this person is listed in B-43.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This group of people that you now mentioned that disappeared in this period, did a Kemal Tulek belong to this group?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Kemal Tulek did belong to this group of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was he, and what can you tell us about him and his disappearance?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: He was a policeman from Foca. I know him. I think he was in solitary confinement in building 3. He was taken out several times for interrogations, and he was interrogated. I think he was beaten, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you think that? Did you see anything on him, or why?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I saw injuries that were typical, typical of blows that are administered with a hand or something else, with certain changes on his face, haematoma. Haematoma in different stages, that is, in different stages of development, I should say. He was taken out towards the end of June 1992, and he is one of the people in this group that went missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's C-25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Ramo Dzendusic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Ramo Dzendusic was in my room, Room 16. I think he was a retiree. I think he had retired before the war. He was interrogated once. He went out of my room for an interrogation. He was terrified, and he said to me that he probably wouldn't survive. And I said, "What does that mean? How come?" And he said, approximately, that they knew quite a few things about him, and that he stood a very slim chance of surviving. He belongs to this group of people who were taken out in June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- before he was taken away in this group and did not return, did he return from beatings? Could you see injuries on him?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: No. I couldn't notice any signs of violence on his face, although he was frightened.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this person is mentioned under C-8 and B-20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of all these men you just mentioned and gave us some details about, did you hear later on after your release that they are missing, or did you never hear anything about them from relatives or other sources?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I personally believe that these people were killed, that they are not alive. Why am I saying this? Because I think -- in fact, I heard a very characteristic sound of a car with a defective exhaust pipe, and this car used to come and go during the night at the time when these people were being taken out of the KP Dom. In a conversation I had later with Witness FWS-210, he told me that he had an opportunity to see that car covered with blood, as he put it. I think it was a caddy type of vehicle produced by the Zastava factory in Kragujevac. After I was released from the camp, I talked to people from Kemal Tulek's family, and they seemed to have information that he was not alive. Some people contacted me about other inmates such as Munib Veiz, Dico, Zulfo Veiz. I had occasion to talk to the man who buried the corpses which flowed downstream towards -- from Foca, and he claimed that he had buried the corpse of Munib Veiz. I don't know whether that is true or not, but in any case, I don't think that these people are still alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this person you mentioned that claimed he had buried Munib Veiz, who would that be? Who was that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I met that person in Sarajevo after being released from the prison. His last name is Subasic. I cannot remember his first name, but I believe he's still alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know the profession of this person?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I think he was a raftsman. He had a raft.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned, you just mentioned the name Dico. I don't -- who is that? We have not yet discussed a person Dico.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: It's a "B," Bico.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I misunderstood you, sorry. Those beatings that you just described, when did they start -- in the evening, I mean, on the days, when did they usually start and when did they usually end?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: A large number of these people were taken away after lunch. Lunch was sometime around 1.00. It took about an hour or two perhaps. So these people were mainly taken away after 3.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these beatings, how long did they last? I'm only referring to this group of beatings that you just described having occurred in the second half of June.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I think the beatings went on until night-time, maybe 10.00 or 11.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you also on the 28th heard shots. Is it only once -- on one evening that you heard the shots or did you hear shots on several occasions?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I think it was the 28th. It could have been in the evening. I can't say what time. There were at least five shots. And in the days that followed I also heard shooting there, but I think those were single shots. But on that day, which I think was the 28th, there were several shots, I think five.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you hear the shots, during the beatings or after the beatings?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: After the beating; during the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall which detainees were taken on this occasion when you heard the shots?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: No. No, I can't say the names with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Do you know a person, a detainee Esad Kiselica?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I know Esad Kiselica. He was in the same room with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was he and what happened to him in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I can't remember how it happened that he found himself in the KP Dom. He was in the room with me and we talked, but I don't remember any more how it came about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was he? Do you know his profession or his age?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: He was middle-aged or elderly, I think. He had his own land. A man from a village, a farmer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kiselica belong to this group of people that disappeared in this second half of June? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: No. I don't think he was in that group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I could have been taken away later, perhaps a month later, which makes it July, but he doesn't belong in this group.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this person is mentioned under C-12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Juso Dzamalija. Do you know him and can you tell us what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I do not know Juso Dzamalija personally, but I spoke to a man who was locked up with him in a solitary cell. I spoke with Zaim Cedic, who had been locked up with him, and Zaim told me that they had been in a solitary cell together in building 3, that guards and soldiers came during the night to beat them on several occasions. He said that Juso Dzamalija got beaten up very badly, purportedly because he had a son who was a policeman. He was in such bad shape mentally that he couldn't go out, and Cedic said that Juso Dzamalija hanged himself on the bars above the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did this happen, do you know, that Dzamalija hanged himself? When did it happen?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I think it was June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you yourself see anything related to this incident?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I didn't see anything, not personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Juso Dzamalija is listed under C-6 and B-17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that Zaim Cedic told you about this. When did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: He was released from solitary confinement, I think, in June 1992, and he was brought to my room, Room 16.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who he was he? Can you tell us where he lived and what profession he had?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: In Tjentiste not far from Foca. He had higher education, I don't know what type, but he worked in the national park of Tjentiste, which is where he was arrested. And he told me he was brought to the police station at Tjentiste, and one of his schoolmates was then chief of that police station, and he beat him the most. From there, he was transferred to the Zelengora Hotel where, allegedly, the Serbian army and Serbian paramilitary formations were based then, the White Eagles and so forth. The drivers who brought him called out to soldiers who came out from the hotel and started beating him. One of those soldiers pulled out a knife and made a cut in his ear. They powered a kilo of salt onto a plate and forced him to eat it, and then they gave him a litre of water to drink. And then they took him away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that he was in the isolation cell in building 3. Was he beaten there as well? Did he tell you anything?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: He said that he had been beaten several times. He said that he had been confused with another man with the same name from Tjentiste. He was taken several times to the gate for interrogation, and he said in these words that Zoran Vladicic had told him it was a mistake, and that they were after another man with the same first and last names. And while he was in solitary confinement, he was beaten several times. He was very frightened. He knew nothing about his family who had fled somewhere towards Tjentiste. He was very pale and very scared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what became of him? Was he also taken away, and is he missing? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: He disappeared in July 1992, in mid-July, and since then has been registered as missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this person is mentioned under B-11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Esad Mezbur?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Esad Mezbur is familiar to me. He was in the KP Dom on one of the upper floors in building 1, but I don't know what happened to him in the end. I believe he was in the group of men who seemed to have been taken Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to be exchanged around the 29th or 30th of August to Rozaje. And that bus seems to have been returned to the KP Dom, and on the next morning the group was split in two groups. One of the subgroups survived, and the other hasn't been heard of. I think he was in that group which did not survive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him in the KP Dom being beaten or with injuries that indicated that he was beaten?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I saw him in the KP Dom, but I didn't notice any signs of violence on his face.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person Hasim Mezbur? Is he related to Esad?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I know there is a person by the name of Asim Mezbur; I don't know of any Hasim. Maybe it's the same person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Asim and Esad, are these different persons?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Asim and Esad Mezbur, those are two different persons, but I don't think there is anyone named Hasim. There is an Asim, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, and what can you tell us about Asim?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: He was in the KP Dom, and I knew him from before. He was a private entrepreneur from Foca. He was said to have been a rich man, and I saw him several times. He was in building 1. I don't know which room. He was on that bus which had set out to Rozaje and then came back to the KP Dom, and the next morning they left the KP Dom again on two buses. He was in one of them, and he was in the group which was later never heard of again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, Esad Mezbur is listed under B-41, and Asim Mezbur is not listed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a Halim Dedovic? Do you know who that was and if he was beaten in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I know Halim Dedovic well. At the time, I was in Room 16. One night the guard simply threw a man into our room. We couldn't see who it was. It was dark. He was badly beaten up. His entire body was swollen. He was very frightened; he was crying. He had a beard and he had a denim jacket and jeans. We recognised him as our barber from Foca, whom we all knew very well. We tried to get him to calm down, but he was very frightened, scared out of his wits, and when he calmed down a little, he told us that for seven days he had been locked up in the basement of the administrative building, as he put it, and he said that there is a metal ring on the concrete floor there somewhere, and he said that he had been beaten. I asked him, "Who beat you?" but he wouldn't tell me. He just said, "I know." I don't think there is anyone whom he told who it was that beat him. The reason seems to have been that he was trying to extinguish the fire at the mosque which was burning. He was trying to save the mosque in Gornje Polje, and they tried to torch it several times. The next morning, they came to his door and picked him up. He disappeared from the KP Dom on the 11th of December, 1992, in a group of 12 men. I remember Aziz Sahinovic, a Slovene journalist, was in that group. What is special about this group is that Aziz Sahinovic was then with that -- in my room, Room 18, together with the barber, and we were later transferred to Room 16. And the night before that, they singled out a group of men and took them to a separate room, and just before dawn, they took them out of the KP Dom. I remember hearing footsteps of the prisoners that morning - I think it was before dawn - the footsteps prisoners who were leaving the KP Dom. It was still dark. Halim Dedovic has never been heard of since. He's registered as missing, together with the other 12 people from that group, including Fahrudin Magdic. I later -- this Fahrudin Magdic was nicknamed Baron. I later asked Gojko about him because I knew they were friends with Baron, and he said that Baron had called him from Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's first return to Halim Dedovic. Was he beaten while he was in the KP Dom, after this incident when you said he was thrown into your room? Was he taken out for our beatings in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: No, not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on this occasion when he was thrown into your room after having been locked up in the administration building, did you see injuries on him?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes. He had injuries on his face at varying stages of development, starting with blue and yellow haematomas around the eye. He had a beard, so you could only see the area around the eye.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this person is listed under 5.23, and I think the witness was just referring to this incident, but he's also listed under A-6 and B-13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. That may be an appropriate time. Now, we're starting off with a videolink witness first thing in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: How long do we expect that witness to take so we can give the doctor the some idea when he can return.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It will probably take the entire day because I assume Defence counsel have a lot of questions to ask from this other witness. So it will probably take the entire day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, I'm sorry we have to interrupt your evidence, but there is a very highly complicated technical procedure we're adopting tomorrow to take the evidence of a witness by videolink. It's fixed for tomorrow, so we will have to return to you on Thursday. But thank you for coming, and we'll see you again on Thursday. Very well. We will adjourn now until 9.30 tomorrow. It's not a closed court, is it? No. That's another one.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, it is closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
